h1: How much do SEO services cost, one service at a time?
metaTitle: How Much Do SEO Services Cost? An INR Rate Card
metaDescription: A real INR rate card for eight SEO services — audits, content, technical sprints, links and local — so you can price your scope before anyone quotes you.
answer: Bought separately in India, a technical audit runs ₹35,000–₹60,000, a researched article ₹6,000–₹18,000, a two-week technical fix sprint ₹60,000–₹1,00,000, and a monthly digital PR campaign ₹40,000–₹1,20,000. Add them up and you get your own scope before an agency builds one for you.
takeaways: A retainer is a bundle. Price the parts first and you'll know whether the bundle is a discount or a markup.
**₹40,000 a month funds about three deliverables. ₹75,000 funds six or seven.** That gap is the difference between doing one thing and running a programme.
Audits, analytics setup and schema rollouts are worth buying once. Content, links and technical hygiene are only worth buying monthly.
When budgets get cut, the first thing dropped is almost always the thing that was working slowest — which is usually links, and usually a mistake.

sections.h2: Why a rate card beats a range
body: Ask what SEO services cost and you'll be handed a range: ₹25,000 to ₹3,00,000 a month. Technically true, practically useless. It's like being told a car costs between two lakh and two crore.

The useful question is what each piece of work costs on its own, because that's the only way to check whether a retainer is fairly priced. A ₹75,000 bundle containing ₹1,10,000 of separately-priced work is a good deal. A ₹75,000 bundle containing ₹35,000 of work is a subscription to somebody's office rent.
So here's the card. Indian market rates, ex-GST, for agencies and senior freelancers who'll show you their previous work. Prices vary by city and by whether the buyer looks like they'll haggle.

callout.body: Analytics and conversion tracking setup — GA4, Search Console, goal and call tracking — runs ₹25,000–₹40,000 once. It's the least exciting line on any quote and the only one that makes every other line provable. Skip it and you'll spend twelve months arguing about whether SEO worked.

sections.h2: What's worth unbundling, and what isn't
body: Some services genuinely make sense to buy once and own. Others are a false economy the moment you take them out of a retainer.
bullets: **Buy once: the audit.** Pay for it. A paid audit is a diagnosis; a free one is a sales document with a diagnosis attached. Buying it separately also lets you take the findings to three agencies and get comparable quotes.
**Buy once: analytics and tracking setup.** It only needs doing properly one time, and it belongs to you afterwards.
**Buy once: schema and Core Web Vitals.** Both are template-level work. Once shipped, they stop costing money and keep paying.

**Buy monthly: content.** Cadence beats volume every time. Four solid pieces a month for a year outperforms fifty in one quarter followed by silence — Google rewards a site that's clearly still alive.
**Buy monthly: links.** Outreach is a relationship business with a long lag. A one-off link campaign is three months of building contacts you then abandon.
**Buy monthly: technical hygiene.** Every release breaks something. A site with an active dev team needs someone watching, permanently.

callout.title: The unbundling trap
callout.body: Unbundle far enough and you become the project manager. Four vendors, four invoices, four people blaming the other three when the traffic doesn't move. Unbundling saves money on discrete work and costs money on continuous work. Draw the line there.

sections.h2: What gets cut first when the budget shrinks — and what should
body: Budgets get cut. Here's the order it usually happens in, and the order it ought to.
numbered: **Cut first, in practice: links.** They're the slowest to show a result, so they look the most optional. They're also the hardest to restart, because the outreach relationships go cold.
**Cut second, in practice: strategy hours.** The account lead gets 'more efficient', which means a junior now runs your account and nobody notices for two months.
**Cut last, in practice: content volume.** It's the most visible output, so it survives longest — even when the pages being published have no search demand behind them.
**What we'd actually cut first: content volume.** Two excellent pieces beat four adequate ones, and the saving is immediate.

**What we'd cut last: technical hygiene and analysis.** They're cheap, they're preventative, and they're the only lines that stop a small problem from becoming a six-month recovery. Ask anyone who's been through [a replatform that killed their traffic](/journal/the-replatform-that-killed-your-traffic).

sections.h2: How to write a scope brief that makes two quotes comparable
body: Most founders receive three proposals that can't be compared, because each agency scoped a different job. Send the same one-page brief to all three and the problem disappears.
Six things it needs. Nothing else.
numbered: **Your site, in numbers.** URL count, CMS, whether you have developers, how many languages, how many locations.
**The one metric you're buying.** Qualified leads from organic search, or organic revenue. Not traffic, not rankings. State today's number.
**Your must-haves, from the rate card above.** Name the services. "SEO" is not a scope; "a technical audit, four articles a month, and GBP work for three locations" is.
**Your budget, honestly stated.** Withholding it doesn't get you a better price, it gets you three proposals aimed at different budgets that you then can't compare.
**Ask for hours by role.** One line per role, per month. This is the single question that separates planned work from hopeful work.

**Ask what happens if it doesn't work.** Then compare the answers rather than the prices. Ours is on [the pricing page](/pricing) — we freeze your trailing-90-day organic lead count on day one and work free past 90 days until we beat it. We never promise a specific ranking position, because nobody controls Google's index.

faqs.q: How much does an SEO audit cost in India?
faqs.a: ₹35,000 to ₹60,000 for a genuine technical and content audit of a site under 500 URLs, more for large catalogues. Free audits are sales documents — automated crawl output with a call booked at the end. Paying for one gets you findings you can take to three agencies.

faqs.q: How much does one SEO article cost?
faqs.a: ₹6,000 to ₹18,000 for a researched, edited 1,200–1,800 word piece. The main driver of the gap is whether anyone interviews a subject-matter expert. Bulk content at ₹1,500 a post exists, ranks rarely, and usually costs more to fix later than it saved.

faqs.q: Can I buy SEO services one at a time instead of a retainer?
faqs.a: For discrete work, yes — audits, analytics setup, schema and speed work are all better bought once and owned. Continuous work isn't: content, links and technical hygiene need cadence, and buying them project by project means restarting from cold every time.

faqs.q: What's the cheapest useful SEO service to buy first?
faqs.a: Analytics and conversion tracking, at ₹25,000–₹40,000 once. It's dull, it ranks nothing, and without it you cannot prove any other spend worked. Second is a paid technical audit, which tells you whether your site is even capable of ranking before you buy content.

faqs.q: Why do SEO service prices vary so much between agencies?
faqs.a: Because the same service name covers wildly different work. "Four blogs a month" can mean four AI drafts or four expert-interviewed pieces. Ask for hours by role and a description of the deliverable, and most of the variance stops being mysterious.

No. Indian agencies quote ex-GST and add 18% on the invoice. A ₹40,000 monthly scope bills at ₹47,200. GST-registered businesses claim it back as input credit, so it's a cash-flow cost — but it still leaves your account first.
